title: Topic vs Subject Particles (은/는 vs 이/가)
subtitle: Contrast and context setting versus grammatical agency and new information
keyPoint: Use 은/는 to establish known topics or draw contrasts, and 이/가 to mark the grammatical subject or introduce brand-new information.

cells: Apples are expensive, but bananas are cheap.

useCases.label: Contrasting Two Items
useCases.example: 커피는 마셔요. 하지만 차는 안 마셔요.

mistakes.note: Interrogative question words like 'who' introduce unknown information and must take 이/가 (forming 누가), never 은/는.

mistakes.right: 선생님은 민수가 아니에요. / 민수는 선생님이 아니에요.
mistakes.note: The complement before the negative copula 아니다 always takes 이/가, not 은/는.
Do not stack subject and topic markers randomly; pick the one that matches whether the noun is the main topic or the specific subject.

quiz.question: Who ordered the coffee? '___ ordered the coffee.' (Focus on identifying the person)
quiz.explanation: When answering 'who' or identifying the agent as new information, use the subject marker 이/가.

quiz.question: 'As for me, I am a student.' Choose the topic marker for 저 (ends in vowel).
quiz.explanation: Nouns ending in a vowel take 는 for the topic marker; 저 becomes 저는.

quiz.question: Contrasting: 'Apples are sweet, but lemons ___ sour.'
quiz.explanation: For contrasting two items (apples vs lemons), use the topic marker 은/는. 레몬 ends in a consonant, so it takes 은.

quiz.question: 'The weather is nice today.' (Today is the topic; the weather is the specific subject).
quiz.explanation: The standard framing uses 오늘은 (topic) and 날씨가 (subject of the adjective 좋아요).

tip: If you are answering the question 'Who did it?' use 이/가. If you are sharing facts about yourself or comparing items, reach for 은/는.

title: Polite Informal Style (해요체: -아/어/여요)
subtitle: Everyday polite speech based on Korean stem vowel harmony
keyPoint: Stems ending in vowels ㅏ or ㅗ take -아요, 하다 verbs become 해요, and all other stem vowels take -어요.

cells: Dark / Other Vowels (ㅓ, ㅜ, ㅣ, ㅡ, etc.)

mistakes.note: 먹다 has the stem vowel ㅓ, which requires -어요, not -아요.
All 하다 verbs contract into 해요 in the polite informal present.
Most ㅂ-final descriptive adjectives drop ㅂ and add -워요 (덥다 → 더워요).

quiz.question: Conjugate 앉다 (to sit; stem has vowel ㅏ) into polite informal style.
quiz.explanation: The last vowel of the stem 앉- is ㅏ, so it takes -아요, becoming 앉아요.

quiz.question: Conjugate 마시다 (to drink; stem ends in ㅣ) into polite informal style.
quiz.explanation: When an open stem ending in ㅣ meets -어요, ㅣ and ㅓ merge into ㅕ (마시 + 어요 = 마셔요).

quiz.question: Conjugate 돕다 (to help; special ㅂ irregular with ㅗ stem) into polite informal style.
quiz.explanation: 돕다 and 곱다 are unique ㅂ irregulars whose vowel ㅗ causes ㅂ to turn into 오, yielding 도와요 (not 도워요).

quiz.question: Conjugate 운동하다 (to exercise) into polite informal style.
quiz.explanation: 하다 regularly contracts to 해요 in standard everyday speech.

tip: Look strictly at the *final vowel* of the verb stem, not consonants, to decide between -아요 and -어요.

title: Copula and Negative Copula (이다 vs 아니다)
subtitle: Stating identity with 이에요/예요 and denying it with 이/가 아니에요
keyPoint: Attach 이에요/예요 directly to a noun to mean 'is', but write 아니다 as a separate word preceded by the subject marker 이/가.

mistakes.note: 사람 ends in a consonant (ㅁ), so it must take 이에요, never 예요.
아니다 always requires the subject particle 이/가, never the object marker 을/를.
Unlike 이다, 아니다 is an independent adjective and needs both a particle (이/가) and a space before it.

quiz.question: Complete the identity sentence: 'This is water (물).' -> 이것은 물___.
quiz.explanation: 물 ends in final consonant ㄹ, so it attaches directly to 이에요.

quiz.question: Complete the denial sentence: 'I am not an employee (회사원).' -> 저는 회사원___.
quiz.explanation: 회사원 ends in consonant ㄴ, so it takes the subject particle 이 followed by 아니에요.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'She is a doctor (의사).' -> 그분은 의사___.
quiz.explanation: 의사 ends in vowel ㅏ, so it attaches directly to 예요.

quiz.question: Complete the denial: 'This is not coffee (커피).' -> 이것은 커피___.
quiz.explanation: 커피 ends in a vowel, so it takes the subject marker 가 followed by space and 아니에요.

tip: Remember: 이다 attaches like glue with no space (사과예요), while 아니다 always keeps a particle and a space (사과가 아니에요).

title: Locative Particles: Static vs Dynamic (에 vs 에서)
subtitle: Distinguishing existence and destination from dynamic actions and source
keyPoint: Use 에 for static existence (있다/없다), destinations (가다/오다), and times; use 에서 for dynamic actions taking place at a location.

mistakes.note: Reading (읽다) is an active dynamic verb taking place in the library, so you must use 에서.

mistakes.wrong: 지금 집에 가고 있어요? 아니요, 방에서 있어요.
mistakes.note: State of existence with 있다/없다 takes the static particle 에.
Drinking coffee is an action occurring at a venue, demanding 어디에서 (or 어디서).

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'I study at the library.' -> 도서관___ 공부해요.
quiz.explanation: 공부하다 is an action taking place at the location, requiring 에서.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'My keys are on top of the desk.' -> 책상 위___ 열쇠가 있어요.
quiz.explanation: The verb 있다 expresses static existence/presence, which takes the particle 에.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'I am going to school right now.' -> 지금 학교___ 가요.
quiz.explanation: Verbs of movement toward a destination (가다, 오다) pair with 에 to indicate destination.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'I came from America.' -> 저는 미국___ 왔어요.
quiz.explanation: When expressing the origin or source ('from a place'), use 에서.

tip: Ask yourself: Is an action happening inside that place? If yes, pick 에서. Is something simply sitting there or heading there? Pick 에.

title: Honorific Subject Infix (-(으)시-)
subtitle: Showing respect to the person performing the action
keyPoint: Insert -(으)시- into verb stems and use suppletive verbs when the grammatical subject is someone who warrants respect.

mistakes.note: Never use the honorific marker -(으)시- to describe your own actions; it is exclusively for honoring others.
먹다 has dedicated suppletive honorific verbs (드시다 / 잡수시다); do not say 먹으시다.
When honoring a person existing in a place, the honorific counterpart of 있다 is 계시다, not 있으시다.

quiz.question: Select the correct honorific form of 보다 (to see/watch; vowel stem).
quiz.explanation: The stem 보- ends in a vowel, so it attaches directly to -세요 to become 보세요.

quiz.question: How do you honorably say 'Grandmother is sleeping'?
quiz.explanation: The verb 자다 (to sleep) changes completely to the suppletive honorific verb 주무시다 (주무세요).

quiz.question: How do you honorably say 'The professor is in the office'?
quiz.explanation: When an honored person exists or stays in a location, use 계시다 (계세요), not 있으시다.

quiz.question: Conjugate 앉다 (to sit; consonant stem) into the polite honorific present form.
quiz.explanation: 앉- ends in a consonant cluster, requiring -으세요 to ease pronunciation: 앉으세요.

tip: Never apply -(으)시- to yourself! It is an elevator for the other person; using it on yourself sounds absurdly self-important.

title: Sequential and Contrastive Connectors (-고, -지만)
subtitle: Connecting thoughts with sequential addition and contrast
keyPoint: Attach -고 or -지만 directly to the verb stem, leaving past-tense markers for the final clause in basic sequences.

mistakes.wrong: 어제 밥을 먹었 고 영화를 봤어요.
mistakes.note: Do not attach the past-tense suffix -었- to the first clause when using -고 for simple chronological order.
Do not combine -고 and -지만 together; attach -지만 directly to the adjective stem.
The polite particle -요 cannot be inserted before the coordinating conjunction -지만 inside the sentence.

quiz.question: Choose the correct connector for 'I washed my hands and ate dinner': 손을 ___ 저녁을 먹었어요.
quiz.explanation: -고 connects two actions chronologically without needing a tense marker on the first verb.

quiz.question: Choose the correct form for 'The price is cheap, but the quality is good': 가격은 ___ 품질이 좋아요.
quiz.explanation: -지만 marks direct contrast ('cheap, but good quality').

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly lists attributes without tense error?
quiz.explanation: In standard coordinate listing, the first adjective stem (맑-) directly takes -고 while tense is marked on the final predicate.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'I studied hard, but the exam was difficult': 열심히 ___ 시험이 어려웠어요.
quiz.explanation: -지만 (or past form -했지만) conveys contrast against the difficult outcome.

tip: Remember: -고 holds the tense in suspense! Put all your tense endings (like -았/었-) on the very last verb of the sentence.

title: Sequential Linker vs Causal Marker (-아/어서 vs -(으)니까)
subtitle: Distinguishing natural consequence from subjective justification
keyPoint: Use -아/어서 for natural chronological cause and effect without imperatives; use -(으)니까 for subjective reasoning, discovery, and commands.

cells: Doing action 2 in the state of action 1

mistakes.note: For a simple factual past consequence, -아/어서 is natural; -(으)니까 sounds overly emphatic unless justifying a decision.
-아/어서 can never precede imperative endings like -(으)세요 or suggestions like -(으)ㅂ시다.
Never attach past tense markers (-았/었-) directly before -아/어서.

quiz.question: Complete the request: 'Since it is dangerous, please do not go': 위험___ 가지 마세요.
quiz.explanation: With imperative commands (-지 마세요), only -(으)니까 is grammatically valid, never -아/어서.

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly expresses 'I went to the library to read'?
quiz.explanation: 가서 denotes sequential action where the subject moves somewhere to perform the second action.

quiz.question: Find the grammatically invalid Korean sentence:
quiz.explanation: -아/어서 cannot be used with an imperative request like 서두르세요 (hurry up).

quiz.question: Complete with natural factual reason: 'I caught a cold, so I rested at home': 감기에 ___ 집에서 쉬었어요.
quiz.explanation: -아/어서 expresses a simple, natural factual cause and outcome in past narrative statements.

tip: Golden Rule: If the clause ends in -세요 (please do) or -자 (let's), immediately eliminate -아/어서 and pick -(으)니까!

title: Noun-Modifying Verb Endings (관형형: -(으)ㄴ, -는, -(으)ㄹ)
subtitle: Transforming verbs into descriptive relative clauses
keyPoint: Action verbs use -(으)ㄴ for past, -는 for present, and -(으)ㄹ for future, while adjectives use -(으)ㄴ for present description.

examples.en: 저기서 신문을 읽는 분이 우리 교수님입니다.

mistakes.note: Adjectives take -(으)ㄴ in the present tense, never -는 (with irregular exceptions like 있다/없다).
Action verbs that describe a completed past event must take -(으)ㄴ, not -는.
Verbs with a ㄹ-irregular stem drop the ㄹ before -는 (살다 -> 사는).

quiz.question: Select the correct phrase for 'The movie I am watching now': 지금 ___ 영화
quiz.explanation: Action verbs modifying a noun in the ongoing present take -는.

quiz.question: Select the correct phrase for 'The book I will read tomorrow': 내일 ___ 책
quiz.explanation: Future or prospective actions modifying a noun take -(으)ㄹ.

quiz.question: Which form correctly modifies the noun with the adjective '작다' (small)?
quiz.explanation: Descriptive verbs (adjectives) take -(으)ㄴ for present state description (작다 + 은 -> 작은).

quiz.question: Fill in the blank with the past modifier of '만들다' (to make): 이것은 제가 어제 ___ 빵이에요.
quiz.explanation: For ㄹ-stem verbs like 만들다, the ㄹ drops before -ㄴ in the past modifier form, yielding 만든.

tip: Watch out for 있다 and 없다! Even though they look like adjectives, they always conjugate with -는 (e.g., 맛있는, 재미없는).

title: Expressing Ability and Possibility (-(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다)
subtitle: Stating capability, potential, and impossibility
keyPoint: Combine the prospective modifier -(으)ㄹ with the defective noun 수 and 있다/없다 to state what one can or cannot do.

cells: 갈 수 있다 / 살 수 없다
먹을 수 있다 / 읽을 수 없다

examples.en: 저는 매운 음식을 잘 먹을 수 있어요.
내일 몇 시에 올 수 있나요?

mistakes.note: The bound noun 수 requires a space before and after: -ㄹ 수 있다.
Use 없다 (not 안 되다) as the pairing with -(으)ㄹ 수 when expressing lack of ability.
The defective noun 수 must always be modified by the prospective ending -(으)ㄹ, never -는.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank for 'I can swim': 저는 수영을 ___ 있어요.
quiz.explanation: 하다 takes -ㄹ 수 to formulate capability: 할 수 있어요.

quiz.question: Which option means 'I cannot eat because it is hot'?
quiz.explanation: Consonant stem 먹다 takes -을 수 없다 for inability/impossibility.

quiz.question: Choose the correct spelling with proper Korean spacing:
quiz.explanation: 수 is an independent bound noun, so it must have a space before and after it: 갈 수 있어요.

quiz.question: What is the irregular ability form for '듣다' (to hear)?
quiz.explanation: ㄷ irregular verb 듣다 changes ㄷ to ㄹ before vowels, yielding 들을 수 있다.

tip: Remember spacing: keep a space between the verb ending -(으)ㄹ and the bound noun 수, and another space before 있다/없다!

title: Intentional and Prospective Endings (-(으)ㄹ게요 vs -(으)려고 하다)
subtitle: Distinguishing conversational promises from premeditated plans
keyPoint: Use -(으)ㄹ게요 to make a spontaneous commitment or promise to your listener; use -(으)려고 하다 to convey a premeditated plan or intention.

useCases.label: Planned Future Intent
useCases.example: 다음 주에 새 컴퓨터를 사려고 해요.

examples.en: 이번 주말에 친구들과 여행을 가려고 해요.

mistakes.note: -(으)ㄹ게요 carries personal volition/promise and can never be used with inanimate subjects or weather forecasts.
-(으)ㄹ게요 can only be used in the first person (I or we), never with third-person subjects.
-(으)ㄹ게요 cannot be used as an interrogative question to ask someone else's will.

quiz.question: Which ending fits a spontaneous promise to a coworker: 'I will prepare the documents'?
quiz.explanation: -(으)ㄹ게요 is used to make a direct promise or offer of action directly to the conversational partner.

quiz.question: Which form describes an existing plan: 'I intend to study abroad next year'?
quiz.explanation: -(으)려고 하다 expresses a premeditated intention or plan formulated prior to speaking.

quiz.question: Why is '마이클 씨가 올게요' ungrammatical?
options: Because 마이클 is a proper noun.
Because -(으)ㄹ게요 can only be used with a 1st-person subject.
Because 올게요 requires an indirect object.
quiz.explanation: -(으)ㄹ게요 is exclusively restricted to first-person statements (I/we will).

quiz.question: Complete the clause: 'I exercise in order to stay healthy': 건강을 ___ 매일 운동해요.
quiz.explanation: -(으)려고 functions as an intentional subordinate linker meaning 'in order to'.

tip: Think of -(으)ㄹ게요 as 'I will do this for you / I give you my word.' Never use it to ask questions or describe what someone else will do!

title: Background Information and Contrast (-는데/-(으)ㄴ데)
subtitle: Provide context, introduce a topic, or signal a soft contrast between two clauses.
keyPoint: Attach -는데 to action verbs and -(으)ㄴ데 to descriptive adjectives to establish premise, context, or mild contrast before the main clause.

cells: I eat, but / as I eat...
I am a student, and / but...

examples.en: 밖은 날씨가 좋은데 바람이 많이 불어요.
저 사람이 우리 선생님인데 정말 친절해요.

mistakes.note: 비싸다 is an adjective (descriptive verb), so it takes -(으)ㄴ데, not -는데.
Action verbs take -는데 in the present tense regardless of whether the stem ends in a consonant or vowel.
Nouns require -인데 rather than -는데 directly.

quiz.question: Which form correctly completes: '날씨가 ___ 외투를 입으세요.' (It is cold, so wear a coat)?
quiz.explanation: 춥다 is an irregular ㅂ adjective; ㅂ changes to 우, producing 추운데 to set the situational background.

quiz.question: Which form correctly completes: '지금 도서관에서 책을 ___ 조용히 해 주세요.' (I am reading a book, so please be quiet)?
quiz.explanation: 읽다 is an action verb, so it takes -는데 in the present tense.

quiz.question: Which form correctly completes: '어제 영화를 ___ 아주 재미있었어요.' (I watched a movie yesterday, and it was very fun)?
quiz.explanation: For past tense background clauses, attach -는데 to the past stem: 보았- + 는데 = 봤는데.

quiz.question: Which form correctly completes: '이것은 내 ___ 빌려줄 수 없어.' (This is my pencil, so I cannot lend it)?
quiz.explanation: Nouns take -인데 to set the background premise.

tip: Remember that adjectives containing 있다/없다 (like 맛있다, 재미없다) exceptionally conjugate with -는데 (맛있는데, 재미없는데) like action verbs.

title: Obligation and Permission (-아/어야 하다 vs -아/어도 되다)
subtitle: Express what you must do, what you are allowed to do, and what is forbidden.
keyPoint: Use -아/어야 하다 for duties ('must'), -아/어도 되다 for permission ('may'), and -(으)면 안 되다 for strict prohibition ('must not').

cells: May go / It is okay to go

useCases.label: Expressing Duty
useCases.example: 내일 시험이 있어서 열심히 공부해야 해요.

useCases.label: Stating Prohibition
useCases.example: 도서관에서 큰 소리로 떠들면 안 돼요.

examples.en: 내일 시험이 있어서 열심히 공부해야 해요.
도서관에서 큰 소리로 떠들면 안 돼요.
수업 시간에 휴대전화를 사용하면 안 돼요.

mistakes.note: To ask for permission ('May I...?'), use -아/어도 되다 rather than the conditional -(으)면 되다.
While 피우지 말아야 돼요 is grammatically possible, standard prohibition ('Do not smoke') is naturally stated with -(으)면 안 되다.
Obligation combines directly with the vowel stem via -아/어야 하다, not with the conditional -(으)면.

quiz.question: Choose the best option: '박물관 안에서는 음식을 ___.' (You must not eat food inside the museum.)
quiz.explanation: Prohibition ('must not') is expressed by verb stem + -(으)면 안 되다. Since 먹- ends in a consonant, 먹으면 안 돼요 is correct.

quiz.question: Choose the best option: '이 컴퓨터를 ___?' (May I use this computer?)
quiz.explanation: Asking for permission uses -아/어도 되다. 쓰다 + -어도 되다 becomes 써도 돼요.

quiz.question: Choose the best option: '비행기 탑승 전에 여권을 반드시 ___.' (You must show your passport before boarding.)
quiz.explanation: Obligation/requirement is expressed with -아/어야 하다 (or 되다). Showing a passport is mandatory.

quiz.question: Choose the best option: '내일은 휴일이라서 회사에 ___.' (Tomorrow is a holiday, so you don't have to come to the office.)
quiz.explanation: Lack of obligation ('don't have to') is formed using -지 않아도 되다 or 안 -아/어도 되다.

tip: In daily speech, -아/어야 되다 is used far more frequently than -아/어야 하다, which often sounds slightly more formal or written.

title: Indirect Quotation Endings (간접 화법: -다고/냐고/라고/자고 하다)
subtitle: Quote statements, questions, commands, and suggestions secondhand.
keyPoint: Report statements with -다고, questions with -(느)냐고, commands with -(으)라고, and proposals with -자고 followed by an utterance verb.

cells: They ask if someone is going

useCases.label: Relaying Instructions / Orders
useCases.example: 의사 선생님이 약을 꼭 챙겨 먹으라고 하셨어요.

useCases.label: Relaying Invitations
useCases.example: 친구가 주말에 영화를 같이 보자고 했어요.

examples.en: 의사 선생님이 약을 꼭 챙겨 먹으라고 하셨어요.
친구가 주말에 영화를 같이 보자고 했어요.
지수가 한국 음식을 정말 좋아한다고 들었어요.

mistakes.wrong: 선생님이 오라고 했어요. (when requesting to give something)
mistakes.note: When the speaker requests an item for themselves in indirect speech, use 달라고 하다 instead of 주라고 하다.
Adjectives take -다고 하다 directly without the present modifier ㄴ/는 that action verbs use.

mistakes.wrong: 친구가 내일 영화를 보라고 했어요. (suggesting we go together)
mistakes.note: Suggestions ('Let's do...') require -자고 하다; -(으)라고 하다 is strictly an order ('You do it').

quiz.question: Which verb form correctly reports the suggestion: 'Let's eat lunch together' (같이 점심을 ___)?
quiz.explanation: Indirect proposals/suggestions ('Let's...') use -자고 하다.

quiz.question: Which verb form reports an order: 'The teacher told me to do my homework' (선생님께서 숙제를 ___)?
quiz.explanation: Indirect commands and imperatives ('Do this') use -(으)라고 하다.

quiz.question: Which verb form reports a question: 'He asked where I live' (어디에 ___ 물어봤어요)?
quiz.explanation: Indirect questions take -(느)냐고 물어보다/하다.

quiz.question: Which verb form reports an adjective statement: 'He said Korean is easy' (한국어가 ___ 했어요)?
quiz.explanation: Adjectives take plain -다고 하다 directly attached to their basic stem (쉽다 -> 쉽다고).

tip: In everyday spoken Korean, -다고 해요, -자고 해요, etc., are almost universally contracted to -대요, -재요, -래요, and -(느)냬요.

title: Derivational Passive and Causative Suffixes (-이/히/리/기-)
subtitle: Distinguish between actions that happen to a subject vs actions caused by a subject.
keyPoint: Derivational suffixes -이-, -히-, -리-, and -기- change active verbs into passive verbs (suffering the action) or causative verbs (making someone do the action).

cells: Context and particles determine passive vs causative
먹히다 is passive (-히-); 먹이다 is causative (-이-)
문이 닫히다: The door closes/is closed
웃기다: To make someone laugh / to be funny

mistakes.note: When the mountain cannot be seen passively, use 보이다 with subject marker 이/가, not 보다 with subject.
To dress someone else, you must use the causative affix -히- (입히다), not the active verb 입다.
The door doesn't close something else; it gets closed, requiring the passive suffix -히- (닫히다).

quiz.question: Which verb completes the passive sentence: '조용한 밤이라 음악 소리가 잘 ___.' (Because it is quiet, the music can be heard well)?
quiz.explanation: The passive form of 듣다 (to listen/hear) uses affix -리- with irregular ㄷ becoming ㄹ: 들리다 (들려요).

quiz.question: Which verb completes the causative sentence: '동생을 ___ 울렸어요.' (I teased my sibling and made them cry)?
quiz.explanation: 울다 takes the causative affix -리- to become 울리다 (to make cry). Past tense: 울렸어요.

quiz.question: Which form completes: '경찰이 도둑을 드디어 ___.' (The police finally caught the thief)?
quiz.explanation: The police are performing the active action of catching (잡다), so the active verb 잡았어요 is needed, not passive 잡히다.

quiz.question: Which verb completes: '도둑이 마침내 경찰에게 ___.' (The thief was finally caught by the police)?
quiz.explanation: The thief undergoes the action passively by the police (경찰에게), taking the passive affix -히-: 잡히다 (잡혔어요).

tip: Pay close attention to particles: Causative clauses typically take an agent with -이/가, a recipient with -에게/한테, and a direct object with -을/를, whereas passive verbs rarely take an object marker -을/를.

title: Expressing Conjecture and Deductions (-나 보다 vs -(으)ㄴ/ㄹ 것 같다)
subtitle: Deduce facts from direct observation versus intuitive guess.
keyPoint: Use -나 보다 when deducing something based on sensory clues or observed evidence, and -(으)ㄴ/ㄹ 것 같다 for general conjecture or polite opinion.

useCases.label: Deduction from Physical Clue
useCases.example: 사람들이 우산을 쓰고 있는 걸 보니 밖에 비가 오나 봐요.

useCases.label: Soft Polite Opinion
useCases.example: 이 옷은 저한테 조금 큰 것 같아요.

useCases.label: Future Conjecture
useCases.example: 하늘이 흐려서 곧 비가 올 것 같아요.

examples.en: 사람들이 우산을 쓰고 있는 걸 보니 밖에 비가 오나 봐요.
불이 꺼져 있는 걸 보니 민수가 벌써 자나 봐요.
이 옷은 저한테 조금 큰 것 같아요.
하늘이 흐려서 곧 비가 올 것 같아요.
사무실에 아무도 없는 걸 보니 다 퇴근했나 봐요.

mistakes.note: -나 보다 is based on observing evidence outside oneself and cannot be used for your own deliberate future actions.

mistakes.wrong: 방이 조용한 걸 보니 자는 것 같아요. (when observing an obvious physical clue)
mistakes.right: 방이 조용한 걸 보니 자나 봐요.
mistakes.note: When deducing explicitly from a concrete clue (like seeing or hearing silence), -나 보다 is more natural and precise than 것 같다.
Descriptive adjectives take -(으)ㄴ가 보다 in the present tense; -나 보다 is for action verbs and past tense.

quiz.question: Which pattern completes: '음식점 앞에 줄이 긴 걸 보니 여기가 맛집___.' (Seeing the long line outside, it appears this is a famous restaurant)?
quiz.explanation: Noun + 인가 보다 expresses a strong deduction based on directly observed evidence (the long line).

quiz.question: Which option is best for a soft, polite personal opinion: '제 생각에는 이 색깔이 더 ___.' (In my opinion, this color seems better)?
quiz.explanation: Expressing one's subjective assessment or softening an opinion politely is best done with -(으)ㄴ 것 같다.

quiz.question: Which form best completes: '전화기가 꺼져 있는 걸 보니 배터리가 ___.' (Seeing the phone is off, it seems the battery died)?
quiz.explanation: The deduction is made in the present about a completed past action based on visible evidence: past stem + -았/었나 봐요.

quiz.question: Which sentence is grammatically unnatural in Korean?
quiz.explanation: You cannot use -나 보다 for your own future states or intended actions because you do not deduce your own feelings by external observation.

tip: Pairing your sentence with '-(으)ㄴ/는 걸 보니까' (Seeing that...) naturally leads into a deduction with '-나 봐요' or '-(으)ㄴ가 봐요'.

title: Retrospective Recollection and Sensory Discovery
subtitle: Reporting direct past observations and unexpected outcomes
keyPoint: Use -더라고요 to share personal past sensory observations with a listener, and -았/었더니 to state how your past action triggered a surprising subsequent result or discovery.

cells: Recalling a direct sensory experience to the listener
커피를 세 잔 마셨더니 잠이 안 와요.
My action caused an immediate physical result
I did something and discovered a new situation
어제 비가 많이 오던데 우산 챙겨요.
Providing background observation or mild contrast

useCases.label: Sharing Past Experience
useCases.example: 어제 그 영화를 봤는데 생각보다 재미있더라고요.

useCases.label: Action Leading to Consequence
useCases.example: 늦게까지 컴퓨터를 했더니 눈이 너무 아파요.

examples.en: 그 친구를 오랜만에 만났더니 정말 반가웠어요.
부산에 직접 가 보니까 바다가 참 예쁘더라고요.
아침에 일찍 일어났더니 하루가 정말 길어요.
민수 씨한테 물어봤더니 벌써 다 알고 있더라고요.

mistakes.note: You cannot normally use -더라고요 to report your own willful actions or internal emotional states, since you experience them directly rather than observing yourself from the outside.

mistakes.wrong: 민수 씨가 운동을 열심히 했더니 살이 빠졌어요.
mistakes.right: 민수 씨가 운동을 열심히 해서 살이 빠졌어요.
mistakes.note: When expressing a cause-and-effect with -았/었더니, the subject of the prior clause must typically be the speaker (first person).
The clause following -았/었더니 must report an already realized fact or observation, not a future conjecture.

quiz.question: Yesterday I tried the spicy stew, and I personally found it really spicy: '어제 찌개를 먹어 봤는데 정말 ___.'
quiz.explanation: The speaker is recounting their own past sensory discovery to the listener, which calls for -더라고요.

quiz.question: I exercised hard all morning, and as a result, my legs feel sore: '아침에 운동을 많이 ___ 다리가 아파요.'
quiz.explanation: The speaker did an action in the first clause that directly caused the result in the second clause, requiring -았/었더니.

quiz.question: I called Jisoo, and it turned out she was sleeping: '지수 씨에게 전화를 ___ 자고 있었어요.'
quiz.explanation: First-person action leading directly to discovering a new state requires -았/었더니.

quiz.question: Choose the naturally formed sentence reporting an observation about someone else:
quiz.explanation: Observing someone else's skill and reporting it retrospectively fits -더라고요 perfectly.

tip: Remember: -았/었더니 requires you (the speaker) to perform the action in clause 1, whereas -더라고요 is strictly for things you witnessed or noticed about others and external surroundings.

title: Nominalization Strategies (-기 vs -는 것)
subtitle: Turning verbs into nouns for wishes, lists, habits, and clausal descriptions
keyPoint: Use -기 for fixed lexical expressions, hopes, checklists, and fixed predicates (like -기 시작하다), but use -는 것 to turn entire descriptive clauses into generalized facts or actions.

cells: General acts, abstract facts, perceptual objects ('the act of...')
Wishes (-기 바라다), lists, headings, and emotions

useCases.label: Describing Hobbies / Habits
useCases.example: 제 취미는 주말마다 산에 가는 것입니다.

examples.en: 매일 아침 조깅을 하는 것은 건강에 아주 좋습니다.
비가 너무 많이 와서 운전하기가 힘들어요.
그 사람이 거짓말을 했다는 것을 알고 실망했어요.
오늘 할 일: 도서관 가기, 방 청소하기, 장보기.

mistakes.note: Aspectual verbs like 시작하다 (to start) and auxiliary constructions like - 전에 (before) exclusively take -기, not -는 것.
When defining an activity or hobby as a predicate noun ('My hobby is doing X'), -는 것 (거예요) is standard in natural conversation.

mistakes.wrong: 이 책은 글씨가 작아서 읽는 것이 힘들어요.
mistakes.right: 이 책은 글씨가 작아서 읽기 힘들어요.
mistakes.note: When paired directly with evaluative adjectives like 쉽다, 어렵다, and 힘들다, the verbal root takes -기.

quiz.question: Choose the natural way to say 'Please be safe' in a card: '항상 몸 건강___ 바랍니다.'
quiz.explanation: The honorific wish formula with 바라다 requires -기를 바랍니다.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Writing an email in Korean is very difficult.' = '한국어로 이메일을 ___ 어려워요.'
quiz.explanation: Ease and difficulty adjectives like 어렵다 and 쉽다 take the pattern -기 (어렵다).

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Did you know that Minwoo moved yesterday?' = '민우 씨가 어제 이사한 ___ 알았어요?'
quiz.explanation: Knowing or not knowing an entire factual event requires clausal nominalization with -는/은 것.

quiz.question: Identify the ungrammatical phrase:
quiz.explanation: Complement clauses before '알다/모르다' must use -는 것, never -기.

tip: Think of -는 것 as a transparent glass box wrapping a whole descriptive sentence ('the fact/matter that...'), while -기 turns the verb into a punchy conceptual badge ('swimming', 'running', 'start to...').

title: Plain Style vs Formal Styles (해라체 vs 하십시오체)
subtitle: Navigating written expository prose, public speaking, and hierarchical registers
keyPoint: Use the plain style (해라체: -(ㄴ/는)다) for non-addressed written texts, essays, and journals, while reserving deferential formal style (하십시오체: -(스)ㅂ니다) for spoken public presentations and direct hierarchy.

useCases.label: Academic Essay or Journal
useCases.example: 현대 사회에서는 정보의 속도가 매우 빠르다.

useCases.label: News & Formal Broadcast
useCases.example: 오늘 저녁 전국에 많은 비가 내리겠습니다.

useCases.label: Written Exam Instructions
useCases.example: 다음 질문을 읽고 알맞은 답을 고르라.

examples.en: 지구 온난화는 인류가 직면한 심각한 문제이다.
모든 참석자는 안내에 따라 자리에 착석해 주십시오.
그 소설가는 매일 아침 일찍 일어나 소설을 쓴다.
자기 개발을 게을리하지 않는 사람이 성공하는 법이다.

mistakes.note: In the plain style, descriptive verbs (adjectives) attach directly in their dictionary form without -ㄴ/는- (재미있다, not 재미있는다).

mistakes.wrong: 논문 결론: 우리는 이 규칙을 지킵시다.
mistakes.right: 논문 결론: 우리는 이 규칙을 준수해야 한다.
mistakes.note: Propositions like -ㅂ시다 are colloquial honorific proposals unsuited for formal academic papers, which require the plain declarative -(ㄴ/는)다.
Written tests and impersonal public directives utilize the plain imperative -(으)라 rather than conversational honorific imperatives.

quiz.question: Select the correct plain style declarative ending for the adjective '행복하다' in an essay:
quiz.explanation: In plain written style (해라체), adjectives take their uninflected basic dictionary form (-다).

quiz.question: How should a written test question command students to 'Write your answer'?
quiz.explanation: Impersonal written exam prompts and formal directives use the plain imperative -(으)라.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank for a business speech to clients: '오늘 와 주셔서 진심으로 ___.'
quiz.explanation: A direct spoken address to an audience of clients requires deferential formal speech (하십시오체: -감사합니다).

quiz.question: Which action verb is incorrectly conjugated into written plain style (해라체)?
quiz.explanation: Action verbs in plain present style require -ㄴ/는다; the correct form is 간다, not the plain root 가다.

tip: Rule of thumb: If you are typing an essay, newspaper article, or personal diary for no specific reader, use -ㄴ/는다. The second you look a listener in the eye or address a live audience, use -(스)ㅂ니다.

title: Hypothetical and Concessive Linkers
subtitle: Nuanced concessions: -느니 차라리, -(으)ㄹ망정, and -다손 치더라도
keyPoint: Use -느니 차라리 to state an extreme alternative is preferable to a bad option, -(으)ㄹ망정 to declare an unyielding stance despite severe hardship, and -다손 치더라도 to concede an extreme hypothetical.

cells: I'd rather do Y than do X
Even if / Although X may happen, never Y
Even granting that X is true...
No matter how much X, how could you Y?

useCases.label: Preferential Refusal
useCases.example: 그런 사람에게 굽신거리느니 차라리 회사를 그만두겠어요.

useCases.label: Steadfast Dignity
useCases.example: 가난하게 살망정 남의 것을 탐내지는 않겠다.

useCases.label: Extreme Concession
useCases.example: 그 말이 사실이다손 치더라도 그렇게 화를 내서는 안 된다.

examples.en: 주말 내내 방에 누워 있느니 차라리 봉사활동을 하겠다.
굶어 죽을망정 부정한 돈은 단 한 푼도 받을 수 없다.
실패로 끝난다손 치더라도 우리는 도전할 가치가 있다.
아무리 바쁘다손 치더라도 건강을 챙겨야 합니다.
이런 저질 물건을 비싸게 사느니 차라리 안 사고 말지.

mistakes.note: -느니 차라리 expresses a strong comparative preference between two active choices, not an environmental cause.
The clause following -(으)ㄹ망정 must contrast resolutely with the extreme adversity of the first clause, usually featuring strong negative determination.

mistakes.right: 그 사람이 온다손 치더라도 기다리지 맙시다.
mistakes.note: -다손 치더라도 attaches to the declarative citation base (-ㄴ/는다손 치더라도 for present verbs) and generally leads to a stance unaffected by that extreme premise.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'I would rather stay up all night than leave this work unfinished.' = '일을 끝내지 않고 ___ 차라리 밤을 새우겠다.'
quiz.explanation: Comparing two undesirable actions and picking the lesser evil ('rather do Y than X') uses -느니 차라리.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Even if I fail, I will never give up on my dream.' = '시험에 ___ 내 꿈을 절대 포기하지 않겠다.'
quiz.explanation: -(으)ㄹ망정 expresses an unyielding, resolute determination despite facing extreme failure or negative odds.

quiz.question: Conceding an opponent's point hypothetically: 'Even granting that you were late because of traffic, you still should have contacted us.' = '차가 ___ 연락은 미리 했어야지요.'
quiz.explanation: -다손 치더라도 hypothetically concedes the prior fact while maintaining the speaker's original criticism.

quiz.question: Choose the sentence that uses -느니 차라리 correctly:
options: 밥을 굶느니 차라리 라면이라도 끓여 먹겠다.
quiz.explanation: Comparing starvation with the less bad option of instant noodles perfectly matches the comparative distaste of -느니 차라리.

tip: -느니 is your 'over my dead body, I would rather...' connector; -(으)ㄹ망정 protects your moral pride and honor; -다손 치더라도 is your high-level debate tool: 'Even if we grant your point, it still doesn't change anything.'

title: Discourse Bound Noun Structures
subtitle: Mastering -는 셈 치다, -는 김에, and -(으)ㄹ 리가 없다
keyPoint: Use bound noun constructions like -는 셈 치다 to act as if an assumed reality were true, -는 김에 to take opportunistic advantage of a planned movement, and -(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 to declare logical impossibility.

cells: To pretend / consider an action done
While you're at it / taking the opportunity
There is no way that... / It's impossible
Absolutely no reason to believe (strong colloquial)

useCases.label: Psychological Framing
useCases.example: 돈을 잃어버렸지만 불우이웃을 도운 셈 쳤어요.

useCases.label: Incidental Opportunity
useCases.example: 서점에 가는 김에 제 문제집도 한 권 사다 주세요.

useCases.label: Logical Impossibility
useCases.example: 정직한 민수가 남을 속였을 리가 없습니다.

examples.en: 속는 셈 치고 그 사람의 말을 한 번만 더 믿어 보세요.
외출하는 김에 쓰레기 봉투를 버리고 올게요.
평소에 성실한 그 친구가 약속을 잊었을 리가 없어요.
친구에게 맛있는 밥을 한 끼 산 셈 쳤습니다.
제주도에 출장 간 김에 관광지도 구경했어요.

mistakes.note: The bound noun construction expressing deduction is overwhelmingly used with negative predicates (없다 or rhetorical 있겠어요?). Saying 'ㄹ 리가 있다' in a simple declarative sentence is ungrammatical.

mistakes.wrong: 일부러 도서관에 가는 김에 친구를 만났어요.
mistakes.note: -는 김에 emphasizes doing a secondary task spontaneously because the primary opportunity presented itself; it clashes with deliberately planned independent tasks marked by 일부러.

mistakes.right: 내가 밥을 사 준 셈 쳐요.
mistakes.note: -는 셈 치다 entails mental reframing or pretending on the part of the speaker; you cannot impose this internal assumption onto another person's basic physical actions without context.

quiz.question: You drop your ice cream and decide to think of it as giving to charity: '좋은 일에 기부___.'
quiz.explanation: Mentally reframing a loss or situation as if another scenario happened is -(으)ㄴ 셈 치다.

quiz.question: Ask a favor since your colleague is already getting up: '커피 타러 ___ 내 것도 한 잔 부탁해.'
quiz.explanation: Doing a secondary action opportunistically while performing a primary action is -는 김에.

quiz.question: Express utter disbelief that a kind friend stole something: '그 착한 친구가 도둑질을 ___.'
quiz.explanation: Expressing logical disbelief ('there is no way that...') requires -(으)ㄹ 리가 없다.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank with the natural expression for taking a leap of faith: '___ 한 번 속는 셈 치고 믿어 봐.'
quiz.explanation: The set phrase '속는 셈 치고' (acting as if deceived / giving the benefit of the doubt) naturally collocates with '그냥'.

tip: Think of '김' as an already rolling snowball (ride the momentum: 'while you're at it'), '셈' as an imaginary mental calculation ('let's chalk it up to...'), and '리' as reason or logic ('there is zero reason why...').
